summary.text: D-Day was the Allied landing in Normandy on 6 June 1944, part of Operation Overlord, and it is the largest seaborne invasion in history.
It began the liberation of France and the rest of Western Europe and laid the foundations for the Allied victory on the Western Front.
Troops landed along five sectors named Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno and Sword, and the Allies had a beachhead at each by the end of the first day.

items.prompt: In the months before the landings, the Allies ran Operation Bodyguard. What was it meant to do?

options.label: Destroy German fortifications along the coast
Mislead the Germans about when and where the main landings would come
Guard Allied ships crossing the Channel
Persuade Hitler to move Rommel away

items.explain: Operation Bodyguard was a military deception to mislead the Germans as to the date and location of the main landings.

items.prompt: Weather on the chosen day is poor, and planners accept a 24-hour delay rather than waiting longer. Why not just wait a few more days?

options.label: Troops were running out of food on the ships
Germany would have learned the plan by then
The landing craft could not stay afloat longer
Moon, tide and time-of-day needs met on only a few days each month

items.explain: The planners' requirements for moon phase, tides and time of day meant only a few days each month would do.

items.prompt: The Pas-de-Calais is the closest point in Europe to Britain, yet the Allies pick Normandy. Why?

options.label: Pas-de-Calais was the most heavily fortified and offered little room to expand
Normandy had many large ports ready for the Allies to use
Pas-de-Calais was too far from Britain for the ships to reach
The Germans had left Normandy completely undefended

items.explain: Pas-de-Calais was most heavily fortified with few chances to expand, while Normandy's broad front allowed several threats at once.

items.prompt: The Normandy coast has no port facilities for unloading supplies. How was this drawback overcome?

options.label: By capturing Cherbourg on the first day
By landing at the Pas-de-Calais instead
By building artificial harbours
By using the ports of Brittany at once

items.explain: The lack of port facilities was overcome through the development of artificial Mulberry harbours.

items.prompt: By the end of the first day on 6 June, how connected were the five beachheads?

options.label: All five were linked into one front
Only two were linked, and all five were not joined until later
None had been linked to any other
Three were linked, and Caen was captured

items.explain: Only Juno and Gold were linked on the first day, and all five were not connected until 12 June.

items.prompt: In 1942 Churchill persuades Roosevelt that the Allies lack forces for a landing in France. Where do the western Allies attack instead?

options.label: In the Mediterranean, where British troops were already stationed
In Norway, to cut off German supply lines
In Brittany, on the French peninsula
In the Pacific, to relieve Soviet forces

items.explain: Instead of returning to France, the western Allies staged offensives in the Mediterranean, where British troops were already stationed.

paragraphs.heading: The day the Allies landed
paragraphs.text: D-Day is the common name for the Normandy landings of 6 June 1944, when Allied troops came ashore by sea and by air on the coast of France. The landings, codenamed Operation Neptune, opened Operation Overlord, the Allied invasion of Normandy during the Second World War. No invasion from the sea has ever been bigger. It started the freeing of France and the rest of Western Europe and set up the Allied victory on the Western Front.

paragraphs.heading: A long wait for a second front
paragraphs.text: After Germany invaded the Soviet Union in 1941, Joseph Stalin kept urging his allies to open a second front in western Europe. Winston Churchill persuaded Franklin D. Roosevelt to put the invasion off, because the Allies did not yet have enough forces. Instead they fought in the Mediterranean, winning in North Africa and then invading Sicily and Italy in 1943. When the three leaders met at Tehran in November 1943, Stalin was promised that the second front would open in May 1944.

paragraphs.heading: Why Normandy
paragraphs.text: Four possible landing areas were weighed: Normandy, Brittany, the Pas-de-Calais and the Cotentin Peninsula. Brittany and Cotentin were peninsulas, where the Germans could block an advance at a narrow neck of land. The Pas-de-Calais is the nearest part of the continent to Britain, so the Germans expected a landing there and fortified it most heavily, and rivers and canals left little room to spread out. Normandy allowed a landing on a broad front that could threaten the port of Cherbourg and open a road toward Paris. Its lack of ports would be solved with artificial harbours called Mulberry harbours.

paragraphs.heading: Tricks and timing
paragraphs.text: In the months before, the Allies ran a large deception, Operation Bodyguard, to mislead the Germans about when and where the main landings would come. Dwight D. Eisenhower commanded the Allied forces, while Erwin Rommel led the German forces and built up defences along the Atlantic Wall. Bad weather forced a 24-hour delay. Waiting any longer would have meant at least two more weeks, since the moon, tides and time of day were right on only a few days each month.

paragraphs.heading: Five beaches
paragraphs.text: Shortly after midnight, heavy bombing from the air and sea began, and 24,000 American, British and Canadian airborne troops landed. The landings from the sea followed at around 06:30 along an 80-kilometre (50 mi) stretch of coast split into five sectors: Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno and Sword. Strong winds pushed landing craft east of their targets, and troops came ashore under heavy fire onto beaches covered in mines, stakes, metal tripods and barbed wire. Omaha, with its high cliffs, saw the most casualties.

paragraphs.heading: What the first day won
paragraphs.text: By the end of the first day the Allies held a beachhead at all five sites, though Carentan, Saint-Lô and Bayeux were still German. Only Juno and Gold were joined up that day, and all five beachheads did not link until 12 June. Caen, a main target, held out until 21 July. The Allies lost no fewer than 10,000 men, of whom 4,414 are confirmed dead, while German losses are estimated at 4,000 to 9,000 men.
